title: Nitro Compounds, Amines and Organometallics

toc.title: 20.2 Amines: classification, preparation, basicity, Hoffmann separation and aniline
20.3 Organolithium, organocopper and organocadmium compounds; the Grignard reagent

html:
Nitrogen appears in this 3-question chapter in two opposite electronic costumes. In a nitro group it is positively polarized, electron-withdrawing and reducible; in an amine it carries a lone pair and behaves as a base/nucleophile.

Organometallic reagents supply the opposite carbon polarity — a nucleophilic carbon — and therefore complete many of the syntheses begun in earlier chapters.

Track oxidation level and carbon count, and most named reactions in this unit stop being isolated facts.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • A nitro compound is R–NO₂ (bond through N); an alkyl nitrite is R–O–N=O. RX + AgNO₂ mainly gives the nitroalkane, while ionic KNO₂ mainly gives the alkyl nitrite — the classic ambident-nucleophile contrast.
  • Primary/secondary nitroalkanes have acidic α-H (nitronate resonance) and dissolve in NaOH; tertiary nitroalkanes do not. Complete reduction (Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl, H₂/Ni) gives a primary amine.
  • Nitrobenzene is made by benzene + conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ (NO₂⁺). Reduction menu: Sn/HCl → aniline; Zn/NH₄Cl (neutral) → N-phenylhydroxylamine; alkaline reducing couples → azoxybenzene/azobenzene/hydrazobenzene depending on conditions; strong-acid electrolytic route → p-aminophenol. –NO₂ is strongly deactivating and meta-directing.
  • Amines are 1°, 2° or 3° by the number of carbon groups on nitrogen. C₃H₉N has four isomers: propan-1-amine, propan-2-amine, N-methyl­ethanamine and trimethylamine.
  • Primary amines are prepared cleanly by reducing nitro compounds, nitriles (RCH₂NH₂) or amides (LiAlH₄); by Hofmann bromamide degradation of a primary amide (one carbon fewer); by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis (avoids over-alkylation); and less cleanly by ammonolysis of RX.
  • Basicity: aliphatic amines > NH₃ >> aniline. In water, methylamines follow (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃ because inductive donation competes with solvation/steric effects. Aniline is weak because its lone pair is delocalized into the ring; electron-withdrawing ring groups weaken it further.
  • Hoffmann separation uses diethyl oxalate: 1° → solid oxamide derivative, 2° → liquid oxamic ester, 3° → no reaction; fractions are then hydrolysed back to amines. Hinsberg's benzenesulfonyl chloride gives the parallel diagnostic separation.
  • Nitrous acid separates amine classes: 1° aliphatic → N₂ effervescence and alcohol mixture; aniline at 0–5 °C → benzenediazonium salt; 2° → yellow oily N-nitrosamine; 3° aliphatic → soluble nitrite salt with no N₂. Only primary amines give the carbylamine test.
  • Aniline is acetylated to acetanilide; diazotized and coupled to azo dyes; and its ring is so activated that bromine water gives white 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. Protect –NH₂ as –NHCOCH₃ before controlled nitration.
  • A Grignard reagent RMgX is made from RX + Mg in dry ether. It behaves as R⁻: acids/water → RH, CO₂ → RCO₂H, HCHO → 1° alcohol, other aldehyde → 2° alcohol, ketone → 3° alcohol, ester (2 equivalents) → 3° alcohol, nitrile → ketone after hydrolysis.
  • Reactivity/selectivity: RLi is more reactive/basic than RMgX; Gilman reagents R₂CuLi and organocadmiums R₂Cd are softer/less reactive — both can convert RCOCl to a ketone without adding again, and Gilman reagents excel at coupling and conjugate addition.

20.1 Nitroalkanes and nitrobenzene

Nitroalkanes: a nitrogen group with an acidic α-carbon

The nitro group is best drawn as a resonance hybrid, R–N⁺(=O)O⁻ ↔ R–N⁺(O⁻)=O, with two equal N–O bonds and powerful –I/–R electron withdrawal. Nitroalkanes are classified 1°, 2° or 3° by the carbon attached to NO₂.

They are distinct functional isomers of alkyl nitrites, where oxygen is attached to carbon.

Laboratory preparation treats a primary (or suitable secondary) alkyl bromide/iodide with silver nitrite in aqueous ethanol: C₂H₅Br + AgNO₂ → C₂H₅NO₂ + AgBr.

AgNO₂ is appreciably covalent, so nitrogen attack is favoured; ionic KNO₂ attacks mainly through oxygen and gives ethyl nitrite.

Industrially, alkanes undergo vapour-phase radical nitration with HNO₃ near 400 °C (useful mixtures of nitromethane, nitroethane and nitropropanes).

Nitroalkanes are polar, relatively high-boiling and sparingly soluble in water. Their signature is the acidity of an α-hydrogen: nitromethane has pKₐ about 10 because the conjugate nitronate anion is resonance-stabilized.

Primary and secondary nitroalkanes therefore dissolve in NaOH, form salts and can be α-halogenated or condensed with aldehydes (the Henry/nitroaldol reaction); a tertiary nitroalkane has no α-H and fails these tests.

With nitrous acid, a primary nitroalkane gives a nitrolic acid whose alkali salt is red, a secondary gives a blue pseudonitrol, and a tertiary gives no colour — the nitro counterpart of the Victor Meyer distinction.

Acidic hydrolysis is powerful but must be worded carefully. Boiling a primary nitroalkane with concentrated HCl gives a carboxylic acid and hydroxylamine.

Under the milder Nef conditions — form the nitronate salt in base, then acidify — a primary nitroalkane gives an aldehyde and a secondary one a ketone.

Reduction is the synthetic headline: Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl or H₂/Ni carries RNO₂ to RNH₂, while Zn/NH₄Cl can stop at an N-alkylhydroxylamine.

Nitrobenzene: preparation, reduction menu and ring behaviour

Benzene is nitrated below about 60 °C with concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄. The active electrophile is nitronium, NO₂⁺. Nitrobenzene is a pale-yellow, bitter-almond-smelling oil; like several nitroarenes it is toxic, oxidizing haemoglobin Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ (methaemoglobinaemia).

Reduction can stop at several oxidation levels, and in alkaline solution partly reduced molecules condense in pairs:

Medium/reagent Main product Reading of the result
Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl or H₂/catalyst Aniline Complete six-electron reduction
Zn dust + NH₄Cl (neutral aqueous) N-Phenylhydroxylamine Reduction pauses before aniline
Alkaline glucose or arsenious oxide/NaOH Azoxybenzene Nitrosobenzene + phenylhydroxylamine condense
Zn/NaOH in methanol; also LiAlH₄ Azobenzene Azoxy compound reduced one stage further
Zn dust + aqueous NaOH Hydrazobenzene N–N single-bond stage
Electrolytic, strongly acidic p-Aminophenol Phenylhydroxylamine undergoes acid-catalysed rearrangement

The school value of the table is the medium, not a claim that every industrial reactor gives one textbook product regardless of stoichiometry.

Nitrobenzene itself resists further electrophilic substitution: –NO₂ withdraws by –I and –R, destabilizing the σ-complex especially for ortho/para attack, so forced nitration gives m-dinitrobenzene and Friedel–Crafts reactions essentially fail (nitrobenzene is even used as an inert solvent for some of them).

Nitro groups are explosophores — TNT is 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene — and nitrobenzene's great constructive use is reduction to aniline for dyes, drugs and polymers.

A Grignard by the mole

Problem. Methyl magnesium bromide is made from 0.3 mol of magnesium with excess CH₃Br, then poured onto crushed dry ice (CO₂) and worked up with acid. How many moles of acid form, and what mass of acetic acid is that?

(M of CH₃COOH = 60 g/mol.) Why must every trace of water be gone before the CO₂ arrives?

Solution. One Mg gives one Grignard, and one Grignard fixes one CO₂: 0.3 mol of CH₃COOMgBr, hydrolysed to 0.3 mol acetic acid, a mass of 0.3 × 60 = 18 g.

Water must be absent because its O–H proton is far more acidic than anything else present: it would protonate the carbanion carbon instantly, giving methane and Mg(OH)Br — the reagent suiciding on the solvent instead of carboxylating.

20.2 Amines: classification, preparation, basicity, Hoffmann separation and aniline

Classification and clean routes to primary amines

Count carbon groups attached to nitrogen: RNH₂ is primary, R₂NH secondary, R₃N tertiary and R₄N⁺X⁻ a quaternary ammonium salt. “Aromatic amine” in the strict reactivity sense means N is bonded directly to the ring (aniline); benzylamine has an insulating CH₂ and behaves as an aliphatic amine.

Amines with N–H bonds hydrogen-bond (less strongly than alcohols), smell fishy at low molar mass and form water-soluble salts with acids — a purification handle used throughout pharmaceutical chemistry.

Route to a 1° amine Carbon-count rule Main caution
Reduce RNO₂ or ArNO₂ Same carbon skeleton Choose the reduction medium; alkaline conditions may dimerize nitrobenzene
RX + excess NH₃ (ammonolysis), then base Same R Product amine is also nucleophilic → 2°, 3° and R₄N⁺ mixtures unless NH₃ is in large excess
Reduce RCN (H₂/Ni, Na/EtOH Mendius, or LiAlH₄) Nitrile C becomes CH₂NH₂; versus RX→RCN this is +1 C overall A clean chain-extension route
Reduce RCONH₂ with LiAlH₄ Same total C; carbonyl C becomes CH₂ Strong hydride tolerates few other reducible groups
Hofmann bromamide: RCONH₂ + Br₂/NaOH One carbon fewer (Ch. 19) Only a primary amide gives the classic reaction
Gabriel synthesis: potassium phthalimide + RX, then hydrazinolysis/hydrolysis Same R RX must be SN2-competent (1°/methyl); aryl halides fail, so not a route to aniline

Aniline is manufactured by catalytic reduction of nitrobenzene. Laboratory alternatives are phenol with NH₃ under forcing catalytic conditions and chlorobenzene with NH₃ under Cu-catalysed high-pressure amination.

Basicity: donation, solvation and resonance compete

A base is compared by the pKₐ of its conjugate acid (pKₐH): the higher the pKₐH, the stronger the base.

Alkyl groups donate electron density and should give 3° > 2° > 1°, but in water the ammonium ions are stabilized by hydrogen-bonding solvation best when they carry more N–H bonds and less steric shielding.

The observed aqueous methyl order is therefore (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃; for ethyl groups Et₂NH > Et₃N > EtNH₂ > NH₃.

In the gas phase, where solvation vanishes, the polarizability/inductive order 3° > 2° > 1° emerges. An examiner who gives no solvent usually expects the aqueous textbook order — read the stem.

Aniline is in another league altogether (pKₐH ≈ 4.6 versus about 10–11 for alkylamines).

Its lone pair is an integral part of the ring π system in the free base; protonation forms anilinium, whose nitrogen has no lone pair left to conjugate, so the base is stabilized relative to its conjugate acid. p-Methyl and p-methoxy groups donate and make aniline a little stronger; p-NO₂ withdraws by –I/–R and makes p-nitroaniline feeble (pKₐH ≈ 1.0).

Benzylamine (pKₐH ≈ 9.3) shows how one CH₂ breaks the conjugation and restores an alkylamine-like base.

Separating and identifying 1°, 2° and 3° amines

Hoffmann's separation shakes the mixture with diethyl oxalate. A primary amine gives a solid dialkyl oxamide; a secondary amine gives a liquid ethyl oxamate (an oxamic ester); a tertiary amine does not react.

Fractional distillation removes the tertiary amine first and then the secondary amine's liquid derivative, leaving the primary derivative as a solid residue. Hydrolysis of each derivative with KOH regenerates its amine.

Hinsberg's test uses benzenesulfonyl chloride in NaOH. A primary sulfonamide still has an acidic N–H and dissolves in alkali; a secondary sulfonamide has no N–H and remains insoluble; a tertiary amine forms no sulfonamide.

Acidification reprecipitates the primary derivative, and vigorous hydrolysis returns the amines.

Cold nitrous acid (NaNO₂ + dilute HCl) is the fastest classifier. A primary aliphatic amine forms an unstable diazonium ion that loses N₂ with brisk effervescence, leaving mainly alcohol-derived products.

A secondary amine gives a yellow oily N-nitrosamine (no gas). A tertiary aliphatic amine simply forms a soluble nitrite salt.

Aniline is the celebrated special case: its diazonium salt survives at 0–5 °C long enough to become synthetic gold (next paragraph).

The carbylamine test (CHCl₃ + alcoholic KOH → foul isocyanide) is positive only for primary amines, aliphatic or aromatic.

Aniline: a weak base with a fiercely reactive ring

Aniline is a colourless oil that darkens in air.

It forms salts with acids, is alkylated (usually to mixtures) by alkyl halides and is acylated smoothly: acetic anhydride gives acetanilide, in which the amide nitrogen is a tamer, still ortho/para-directing donor.

Benzoyl chloride in aqueous NaOH gives benzanilide under Schotten–Baumann conditions.

Diazotization at 0–5 °C with NaNO₂/HCl gives benzenediazonium chloride.

Warming with water replaces N₂⁺ by OH (phenol); CuCl or CuBr gives chloro-/bromobenzene (Sandmeyer); KI gives iodobenzene; hypophosphorous acid replaces the group by H; and coupling with phenol in mild alkali or with β-naphthol gives orange to red azo dyes.

The diazonium group is thus a removable steering wheel fixed to the ring through aniline.

Free –NH₂ activates the ring so strongly that bromine water instantly precipitates white 2,4,6-tribromoaniline. Direct nitration is messy: acid oxidizes aniline and converts much of it to meta-directing anilinium.

The examination solution is protection — acetylate to acetanilide, nitrate (para major), then hydrolyse.

Concentrated H₂SO₄ and heat ultimately give sulfanilic acid (p-aminobenzenesulfonic acid, an internal salt important in dye and drug history), while Friedel–Crafts reactions fail because the basic nitrogen binds the Lewis-acid catalyst.

Worked example 20.1 — classify C₃H₉N without a spectrum

Problem. Four isomeric amines C₃H₉N are available. Sample A gives brisk N₂ with cold HNO₂ and a foul carbylamine odour. Sample B gives a yellow oil with HNO₂ and no gas. Sample C gives neither result. Classify A–C.

Solution. A is a primary amine (propan-1-amine or propan-2-amine; the two tests fix the class, not the skeleton). B is the only secondary isomer, N-methylethanamine. C is trimethylamine, tertiary.

One gas syringe and one unforgettable smell have done the work of a spectrum — provided the class logic was learned, not the odour by experience.

Worked example — the aqueous basicity order of ethylamines

Predict the order of basic strength in water: ethylamine, diethylamine, triethylamine, ammonia.

Three effects compete:(a) the +I (inductive) effect of alkyl groups pushes electrons toward nitrogen: 3° > 2° > 1°;(b) solvation of the conjugate acid by hydrogen bonding is best for the least crowded ion: 1° > 2° > 3°;(c) steric hindrance also increases with substitution. Balancing them for ethylamines in water gives (C₂H₅)₂NH > (C₂H₅)₃N > C₂H₅NH₂ > NH₃.

The traps: in the gas phase (no solvation) the order is purely inductive, 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃; and aniline is far weaker than all of these because its lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.

Trap — three reductions/amines tests that swap in MCQs

The carbylamine (foul-smelling isocyanide) test is given by primary amines only; Hoffmann bromamide converts an amide into an amine with one carbon fewer (the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate); and aniline's diazotisation must be done at 0–5 °C — the diazonium salt decomposes (to phenol, releasing N₂) if the mixture warms up.

20.3 Organolithium, organocopper and organocadmium compounds; the Grignard reagent

An organometallic compound contains a direct carbon–metal bond. Because carbon is more electronegative than Li, Mg, Cu or Cd, that bond is polarized Cδ−–Mδ+, making carbon behave as a nucleophile/strong base. The art is choosing the metal to tune ferocity.

Organolithium reagents (RLi) are made from an organic halide and lithium metal in dry ether or hydrocarbon, or by halogen–lithium exchange.

They often exist as aggregates and are more reactive and more strongly basic than Grignard reagents.

They are protonated instantly by water/alcohols to RH, add to carbonyl compounds and CO₂, deprotonate weak C–H acids and exchange with aryl/vinyl halides. n-BuLi solutions can ignite in air; “dry and inert atmosphere” is a safety instruction, not a style preference.

Organocopper reagents used at this level are chiefly lithium diorganocuprates, R₂CuLi (Gilman reagents), from 2 RLi + CuI.

Copper makes carbon softer and more selective: a Gilman reagent couples with an alkyl/aryl/vinyl halide to form a C–C bond (Corey–House synthesis, one route to unsymmetrical alkanes that Wurtz cannot manage cleanly), converts an acid chloride to a ketone and stops, and adds 1,4 (conjugate) to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl where a Grignard reagent often adds 1,2 to C=O.

Organocadmium reagents (R₂Cd) are made by transmetallation, 2 RMgX + CdCl₂ → R₂Cd + 2 MgXCl. They are still less reactive: acid chlorides are converted to ketones, but the ketone/ester/nitrile functions are largely left alone.

That selectivity made them textbook favourites; cadmium's severe toxicity (Ch. 15) means modern laboratories prefer cuprates or organozinc reagents, a good example of methodology changing under toxicology.

The Grignard reagent

Magnesium turnings react with RX in rigorously dry ether or THF to give RMgX. Iodides and bromides form most readily; aryl/vinyl bromides work, chlorides may need THF/initiation.

The solution contains solvated species in Schlenk equilibrium (2 RMgX ⇌ R₂Mg + MgX₂), but the school formula RMgX captures its chemistry: treat R as a carbanion equivalent.

Grignard partner After aqueous workup Carbon-count lesson
H₂O, ROH, RCO₂H, terminal alkyne (any acidic H) RH (the reagent is destroyed) Why solvents/substrates must be dry and proton-free
D₂O RD A clean way to label one C–H position
CO₂ (dry ice), then H₃O⁺ RCO₂H +1 carbon
Methanal (HCHO) RCH₂OH, primary alcohol +1 carbon
Any other aldehyde Secondary alcohol New C–C bond at carbonyl carbon
Ketone Tertiary alcohol Three carbon groups on carbinol C
Ester with 2 RMgX Tertiary alcohol (formate ester gives secondary) The ketone formed first is attacked again
Nitrile, then hydrolysis Ketone Addition stops at an imine salt until workup
Epoxide (oxirane) Primary alcohol after ring opening at the less hindered carbon +2 carbons from ethylene oxide
Sulfur, then workup Thiol RSH Electrophilic heteroatoms also accept R

Two limitations decide many synthesis questions.

A Grignard reagent cannot be prepared from a halide that also carries an acidic proton (–OH, –NH, –CO₂H, terminal –C≡CH) or a carbonyl/ nitro group, because the reagent would attack its own precursor.

And because acid chlorides and esters pass through a ketone stage, excess RMgX adds twice; use R₂Cd or R₂CuLi when the ketone itself is the target.

Choose the metal by stopping power

Want maximum force/basicity? RLi. General carbon nucleophile? RMgX. Need to stop at a ketone or couple two carbons? R₂CuLi (or the older, toxic R₂Cd of the textbooks).

Worked example — predicting Grignard products by the carbonyl type

CH₃–MgBr reacts first by addition to the carbonyl carbon; water (work-up) then protonates the alkoxide. So ask what the carbonyl compound is:

  • With formaldehyde (HCHO): CH₃–CH₂–OH — a primary alcohol (ethanol), one carbon added.
  • With any other aldehyde (e.g. ethanal): a secondary alcohol, CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₃.
  • With a ketone (e.g. propanone): a tertiary alcohol, (CH₃)₃C–OH.
  • With CO₂ (dry ice): after hydrolysis, a carboxylic acid with one extra carbon — CH₃–COOH.

One mechanism (nucleophilic addition of the carbanion-like CH₃⁻) predicts all four answers — and also why the reagent is destroyed by water, alcohol or any –OH/–NH compound (it simply grabs the proton, giving methane).

Common mistake

Five swaps the paper loves here: AgNO₂ gives the nitroalkane, KNO₂ the alkyl nitrite — same anion, two mouths; Sn/HCl gives aniline but Zn/NaOH gives azobenzene and Zn/NH₄Cl the hydroxylamine — the medium steers the reduction; amine classes count carbons on nitrogen, amide classes count carbonyls on nitrogen; the carbylamine and diazotisation tests need a primary amine's N–H hydrogens, which secondary and tertiary lack; and any acidic hydrogen — water, alcohol, terminal alkyne — kills a Grignard, so dry ether is not a preference but a condition of existence.

Chapter summary

  • The nitro group withdraws electrons, acidifies an α-C–H and can be reduced all the way to an amine or stopped/dimerized at intermediate oxidation levels by choosing the medium.
  • Nitrobenzene's ring is deactivated and meta-directing, in complete contrast to the aniline produced from it.
  • Primary-amine synthesis is an exercise in carbon bookkeeping: nitrile reduction extends, Hofmann degradation shortens, and Gabriel protects nitrogen from over-alkylation.
  • Aqueous basicity balances alkyl donation against solvation; resonance makes aniline and especially p-nitroaniline feeble bases.
  • Hoffmann and Hinsberg separations exploit the presence or absence of N–H bonds; nitrous acid and the carbylamine reaction identify amine class in test tubes.
  • Diazotization converts aniline into a versatile leaving group for phenols, haloarenes and azo dyes, while ring protection tames aniline for controlled substitution.
  • Organometallic carbon is nucleophilic: lithium gives force, magnesium gives generality, and copper/cadmium give the selectivity needed to stop at ketones or form chosen C–C bonds.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (d) — R–NO₂ versus the nitrite connectivity R–O–N=O.

2. (a) — covalent AgNO₂ delivers attack through nitrogen; KNO₂ reverses the major site.

3. (c) — deprotonation gives a resonance-stabilized nitronate salt.

4. (b) — NO₂ is reduced by six electrons to NH₂.

5. (a) — mixed acid generates NO₂⁺ and absorbs the water formed.

6. (d) — isolated as anilinium salt until the mixture is basified.

7. (b) — neutral conditions stop at the hydroxylamine oxidation level.

8. (c) — ortho/para σ-complexes place positive charge where –NO₂ destabilizes it most.

9. (b) — amine class counts groups on N, not the class of the attached carbon.

10. (a) — two primary, one secondary and one tertiary isomer.

11. (d) — the imide nitrogen is alkylated once, then the amine is released.

12. (c) — strongly alkaline bromine first N-brominates the amide.

13. (a) — the nitrile carbon is reduced to CH₂NH₂.

14. (c) — the differing physical states of the oxalate derivatives make the separation.

15. (b) — PhSO₂Cl; sulfonyl, not carbonyl, chemistry.

16. (d) — an aliphatic diazonium ion cannot survive loss of N₂.

17. (c) — N-nitrosamines are the classic yellow oils (and notable carcinogens).

18. (b) — two N–H bonds are needed to reach the isocyanide product.

19. (a) — diazonium salts decompose on warming, especially when dry.

20. (d) — all activated ortho/para positions are brominated.

21. (b) — N-acetylation; the amide product is much less basic than aniline.

22. (d) — ether/THF solvates Mg and contains no acidic proton.

23. (c) — carboxylation inserts one carbon as –CO₂H.

24. (a) — lithium diorganocuprate, from 2 RLi + CuI.

25. (c) — R₂Cd is too mild to add to the ketone product appreciably.

  1. Compare the basicity of amines, the Hinsberg test and the distinction between primary, secondary and tertiary amines. [10]

Model answer D1: amines (10 marks)

Introduction. Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one, two or three hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, giving primary (1^{\circ}), secondary (2^{\circ}) and tertiary (3^{\circ}) amines.

The nitrogen is sp³ with a lone pair, which makes amines basic and nucleophilic.

Basicity. In water, the order of \text{p}K_b values shows the basic strength:

Compound Basic strength in water Reason
(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH} strongest +I and good solvation
(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_3\text{N} and \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 strong the 3^{\circ} amine has less solvation of its ion
\text{NH}_3 weaker no alkyl group
\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 very weak the lone pair is delocalised into the ring

So in water for the ethyl amines, 2^{\circ} > 3^{\circ} > 1^{\circ} > \text{NH}_3, and for the methyl amines 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ} > 3^{\circ} > \text{NH}_3.

The aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia, and electron-donating groups (such as -\text{CH}_3) increase the basic strength while electron-withdrawing groups (-\text{NO}_2) reduce it.

Preparation. Reduction of nitro compounds (\text{Sn/HCl} or \text{H}_2/\text{Ni}), reduction of nitriles and amides, Hofmann bromamide degradation (\text{RCONH}_2 + \text{Br}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \to \text{RNH}_2 + \ldots, which gives an amine with one carbon fewer), ammonolysis of haloalkanes and the Gabriel phthalimide synthesis (pure 1^{\circ} amines only).

Distinction of amines.

Test 1^{\circ} 2^{\circ} 3^{\circ}
Hinsberg (benzenesulphonyl chloride, NaOH) sulphonamide, soluble in alkali sulphonamide, insoluble no reaction
HNO₂ (cold) N₂ gas, alcohol yellow oily nitrosamine soluble salt
Carbylamine (CHCl₃, KOH) foul-smelling isocyanide no no
Acetylation yes yes no

Aniline. It is activated in the ring by -\text{NH}_2, so it gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline with bromine water. Direct nitration gives a mixture, since -\text{NH}_3^+ forms in acid and directs meta, so the amine is first protected by acetylation.

Numerical. In the Hofmann reaction of propanamide (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CONH}_2), the product is ethylamine (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2), one carbon fewer.

From 7.3\ \text{g} (0.1\ \text{mol}) of propanamide, the theoretical yield is 0.1\ \text{mol} = 4.5\ \text{g}. Aniline from 12.3\ \text{g} of nitrobenzene (0.1\ \text{mol}) gives 9.3\ \text{g} at a yield of 100\%.

Conclusion. Alkyl groups raise basicity but the aryl group lowers it, and the Hinsberg test with nitrous acid distinguishes the three classes.

Model answer D2: diazonium salts, nitro compounds and Grignard reagents (10 marks)

Introduction. Diazonium salts \text{ArN}_2^+\text{X}^- are the most useful intermediates in aromatic chemistry.

Diazotisation. Aniline reacts with NaNO₂ and HCl at 0 to 5^{\circ}\text{C} to give benzenediazonium chloride. It decomposes above 5^{\circ}\text{C} (to phenol and N₂), so it is prepared cold and used at once.

Reactions of diazonium salts.

  1. Replacement by -\text{Cl}, -\text{Br}, -\text{CN} (Sandmeyer) with CuCl, CuBr and CuCN, and the Gattermann reaction with Cu powder and HX.
  2. Replacement by -\text{I} with KI, and by -\text{F} by heating the tetrafluoroborate (Balz-Schiemann).
  3. Replacement by -\text{OH} by warming with water, and by -\text{H} with \text{H}_3\text{PO}_2.
  4. Coupling reaction. With phenol (alkaline) or aniline (weakly acidic) at the para position, benzenediazonium chloride gives coloured azo dyes (-\text{N=N}-), as in the orange dye of p-hydroxyazobenzene and methyl orange.

Nitro compounds. Nitromethane and nitrobenzene have the -\text{NO}_2 group.

Nitrobenzene is made from benzene with the nitrating mixture and is reduced to aniline: in acid medium with Sn/HCl to aniline, in neutral medium to phenylhydroxylamine, and in alkaline medium to azobenzene.

Aliphatic nitro compounds with \alpha-hydrogen show tautomerism (the aci form). Trinitrotoluene (TNT) and picric acid are explosives.

Grignard reagent. Prepared as \text{RX} + \text{Mg} \to \text{RMgX} in dry ether, because water destroys it (\text{RMgX} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{RH} + \text{Mg(OH)X}). The C-Mg bond is highly polar, so the carbon is a carbanion-like nucleophile.

Reactant Product after hydrolysis
HCHO primary alcohol (one carbon more)
Other aldehydes secondary alcohol
Ketones tertiary alcohol
CO₂ carboxylic acid
Ethylene oxide primary alcohol (two carbons more)
Acid chloride / ester tertiary alcohol

Numerical. \text{CH}_3\text{MgBr} with acetone gives, after hydrolysis, 2-methylpropan-2-ol (\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{COH}, 74\ \text{g mol}^{-1}), so 0.1\ \text{mol} of acetone gives at most 7.4\ \text{g}.

For aniline to chlorobenzene via the Sandmeyer reaction, 9.3\ \text{g} (0.1\ \text{mol}) gives 11.3\ \text{g} of chlorobenzene at best.

Conclusion. Diazonium salts, made cold, allow the introduction of -\text{X}, -\text{CN}, -\text{OH} and azo groups, and Grignard reagents build new C-C bonds under dry conditions.
